{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''tensor-hom adjunction''' is the statement that the [[Tensor product of modules|tensor product]] <math>- \otimes X</math> and [[Hom functor|hom-functor]] <math>\operatorname{Hom}(X,-)</math> form an [[adjoint pair]]:
:<math>\operatorname{Hom}(Y \otimes X, Z) \cong \operatorname{Hom}(Y,\operatorname{Hom}(X,Z)).</math>

This is made more precise below.  The order of terms in the phrase "tensor-hom adjunction" reflects their relationship: tensor is the left adjoint, while hom is the right adjoint.

==General statement for modules==
Say ''R'' and ''S'' are (possibly noncommutative) [[Ring (mathematics)|rings]], and consider the right [[module (mathematics)|module]] categories (an analogous statement holds for left modules):

:<math>\mathcal{C} = \mathrm{Mod}_S\quad \text{and} \quad  \mathcal{D} = \mathrm{Mod}_R .</math>

Fix an <math>(R,S)</math>-bimodule <math>X</math> and define functors <math>F \colon \mathcal D \rightarrow \mathcal C</math> and <math>G \colon \mathcal C \rightarrow \mathcal D</math> as follows:

:<math>F(Y) = Y \otimes_R X \quad \text{for } Y \in \mathcal{D}</math>

:<math>G(Z) = \operatorname{Hom}_S (X, Z) \quad \text{for } Z \in \mathcal{C}</math>

Then <math>F</math> is left [[Adjoint functors|adjoint]] to <math>G</math>.  This means there is a [[natural isomorphism]]

:<math>\operatorname{Hom}_S (Y \otimes_R X, Z) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_R (Y , \operatorname{Hom}_S (X, Z)).</math>

This is actually an isomorphism of [[abelian group]]s.  More precisely, if <math>Y</math> is an <math>(A,R)</math>-bimodule and <math>Z</math> is a <math>(B,S)</math>-bimodule, then this is an isomorphism of <math>(B,A)</math>-bimodules.  This is one of the motivating examples of the structure in a closed [[bicategory]].<ref name="MaySigurdsson">
{{cite book |title=Parametrized Homotopy Theory |last1=May |first1=J.P. |author-link1=J. Peter May |last2=Sigurdsson |first2=J. |year=2006 |publisher=A.M.S. |isbn=0-8218-3922-5 |page=253}}
</ref>

==Counit and unit==

Like all adjunctions, the tensor-hom adjunction can be described by its counit and unit [[natural transformation]]s.  Using the notation from the previous section, the counit

:<math>\varepsilon : FG \to 1_{\mathcal{C}}</math>

has [[natural transformation#Definition|component]]s

:<math>\varepsilon_Z : \operatorname{Hom}_S (X, Z) \otimes_R X \to Z</math>

given by evaluation:  For 

:<math>\phi \in \operatorname{Hom}_S (X, Z) \quad \text{and} \quad x \in X,</math>

:<math>\varepsilon(\phi \otimes x) = \phi(x).</math>

The [[natural transformation#Definition|component]]s of the unit

:<math>\eta : 1_{\mathcal{D}} \to GF</math>

:<math>\eta_Y : Y \to \operatorname{Hom}_S (X, Y \otimes_R X)</math>

are defined as follows: For <math>y</math> in <math>Y</math>,

:<math>\eta_Y(y) \in \operatorname{Hom}_S (X, Y \otimes_R X)</math>

is a right <math>S</math>-module homomorphism given by 

:<math>\eta_Y(y)(t) = y \otimes t \quad \text{for } t \in X.</math>

The [[Adjoint_pair#Definition_via_counit–unit|counit and unit equations]] can now be explicitly verified.  For <math>Y</math> in <math>\mathcal{D}</math>, 

:<math>
\varepsilon_{FY}\circ F(\eta_Y) : 
Y \otimes_R X \to 
\operatorname{Hom}_S (X , Y \otimes_R X) \otimes_R X \to
Y \otimes_R X
</math>

is given on [[Simple_tensor#Tensor_rank|simple tensor]]s of <math>Y \otimes X</math> by

:<math>\varepsilon_{FY}\circ F(\eta_Y)(y \otimes x) = \eta_Y(y)(x) = y \otimes x.</math>

Likewise, 

:<math>G(\varepsilon_Z)\circ\eta_{GZ} :
\operatorname{Hom}_S (X, Z) \to 
\operatorname{Hom}_S (X, \operatorname{Hom}_S (X , Z) \otimes_R X) \to
\operatorname{Hom}_S (X, Z).
</math>

For <math>\phi</math> in <math> \operatorname{Hom}_S (X, Z)</math>'',''   

:<math>G(\varepsilon_Z)\circ\eta_{GZ}(\phi)</math>

is a right <math>S</math>-module homomorphism defined by

:<math>G(\varepsilon_Z)\circ\eta_{GZ}(\phi)(x) = \varepsilon_{Z}(\phi \otimes x) = \phi(x)</math>

and therefore

:<math>G(\varepsilon_Z)\circ\eta_{GZ}(\phi) = \phi.</math>

== The Ext and Tor functors==
The [[Hom functor]] <math>\hom(X,-)</math> commutes with arbitrary [[Limit (category theory)|limits]], while the tensor product <math>-\otimes X</math> functor commutes with arbitrary colimits that exist in their domain category. However, in general, <math>\hom(X,-)</math> fails to commute with colimits, and <math>-\otimes X</math> fails to commute with limits; this failure occurs even among finite limits or colimits. This failure to preserve short [[exact sequence]]s motivates the definition of the [[Ext functor]] and the [[Tor functor]].

== In arithmetic ==
{{Context|section|details=It should be clarified how this is related to the adjunction described so far, which is formulated for modules only. Cf. [[Closed monoidal category]]|date=March 2026}}
{{see also|Currying}}
We can illustrate the tensor-hom adjunction in the [[Category (mathematics)|category]] of [[Function_(mathematics)|functions]] of finite [[Set_(mathematics)|sets]]. Given a set <math>N</math>, its [[Hom functor]] takes any set <math>A</math> to the set of functions from <math>N</math> to <math>A</math>. The [[isomorphism class]] of this set of functions is the [[natural number]] <math>A^N</math>. Similarly, the tensor product <math>- \otimes N</math> takes a set <math>A</math> to its [[cartesian product]] with <math>N</math>. Its isomorphism class is thus the natural number <math>AN</math>. 

This allows us to interpret the isomorphism of [[Hom-set|hom-sets]] 

:<math>\operatorname{Hom}(Y \otimes X, Z) \cong \operatorname{Hom}(Y,\operatorname{Hom}(X,Z)).</math>

that [[universal property|universally characterizes]] the tensor-hom adjunction, as the [[Categorification|categorification]] of the remarkably basic [[Laws of exponents|law of exponents]]

:<math>Z^{YX}=(Z^X)^Y.</math>
